questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14065566/assets/2edd37e6318a7d78b3e6f496bb3f688d006949ccab983f75cece9993817f6b69.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

where we used the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta , \\ y & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

where we used the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & =(3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =3\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

where we used the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =(-5{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =10\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2) \\  & =-5\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{-5\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{5\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

For the polar curve $r=6-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ shown above, calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ as a function of $\theta .$ Fill in the missing parts in the result below.

| $\text{d}y$ | $=$ | {{field-1}}
$\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{d}x$ |  | $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,-$
{{field-2}}
$\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ |
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=6-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(6-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =(6-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\end{aligned}
$$

where we used the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =6{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′}-{({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =6(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{′} \\  & =6{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′}-\frac{1}{2}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{′} \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ).$ Also, since $r=-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dx}{d\theta } & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ))}{-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}{-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )} \\  & =-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\,{sec}^{3}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$

$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,y=3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=2,$ given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ).$ Also, since $r=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dx}{d\theta } & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ))}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡(\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{csc}^{3}⁡(\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r =-2 \cos\theta,$ shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r=-2\cos\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

where we used the identity $\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta.$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =(-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-2\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{′} \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta.$ 

Using the fact that $r=5,$ we get

$$
x =5\cos\theta, \qquad y=5\sin\theta.
$$

Then, to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
x'(\theta) = -5\sin\theta, \qquad y'(\theta) = 5\cos\theta.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{ 5\cos\theta }{  -5\sin\theta} =-\cot\theta .
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}{-5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta  \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}{csc}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
